\paragraph{Drafter's summary.} logit P(churn) = -1.30 + a sparse linear backbone over 29 inputs (voicemail plan -1.12 per SD, international plan +0.83, voicemail messages +0.62, evening charge +0.35, international minutes +0.34, state offsets) + a customer-service-calls threshold (two hinges: nothing for 0-2 calls, then about +2.4 logit per call from 4) + two day-usage hinges (nothing below about 210 day minutes, then steeply up, +4.3 logit above 280 minutes; the 3118 hinge only for customers without voicemail messages, the 10131 hinge off in state:47) + a small evening-minutes hinge and exact state:39/state:15 offsets, all additive in the logit. Day minutes and service calls have no linear term. Train AUC 0.891, accuracy 0.888. Compared with the run's cluster-1 lead (churn100-s4, key 24573), the same two thresholds (service calls, high day usage) carry the nonlinearity, but here day usage is gated by voicemail messages and state:47 rather than combined with evening minutes.

\paragraph{What resisted explanation.} Nothing structural: no hidden node needed splitting (5 input splits, 1 consolidation of the customer-service-calls copies). 6089 (state:18 / 21+ voicemail messages) has logit weight 0.005 (at most +0.05): negligible. The state:39 pair (1295 -$>$ 7872) is a constant -2.33 logit switched off for state:39, almost cancelling state:39's direct -2.61 (net -0.25 vs empirical -0.93). The service-call threshold is placed right (3 -$>$ 4 calls) but the model under-predicts at 4 calls (0.33 vs 0.44) and is over-confident from 5 calls (0.75-0.99 vs 0.55-0.68; 119 customers). state:18 gets +0.41 logit against an empirical -0.48 (65 rows). closed\_\allowbreak{}form\_\allowbreak{}max\_\allowbreak{}abs\_\allowbreak{}err 0.020 (vmail\_\allowbreak{}state18\_\allowbreak{}unit) is 3-significant-figure rounding; numeric error 1.8e-15.

\subsection{Plain-language summary}\label{app:churn100-s4-c2:plain}
\noindent{\small\textit{AI-assisted draft for review (unverified). Each sentence cites the claims (C01, C02, \ldots) that back it; every cited claim was computed on the model and the training split and passed its automatic checks. Magnitudes are changes in predicted risk for a typical patient; confidence words follow the test-split check and n. The text describes what the model does, not the world.}}\par\smallskip
\paragraph{Summary (drafted).} For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, no international or voice-mail plan, no voice-mail messages, 1 call to customer service and median usage) the model predicts a chance of leaving of about 3\%; it adds up six parts: fixed-weight inputs, service calls, heavy daytime use, state units, an evening unit and a small voice-mail unit.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C046]}} This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights: an international plan raises a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 3\% to about 31\%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C047, C051]}} More voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 3\% at 0 to about 10\% at 32 messages, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C049]}} A higher evening charge and more international minutes also raise it steadily, each from about 2\% to about 4\% across their usual range.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C055, C056]}} Through it, the state moves the chance from about 3\% in West Virginia to about 11\% in Washington and about 7\% in New Jersey, and to under 1\% in Hawaii and in Rhode Island (72 to 122 training customers per state).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C048, C050, C052, C053]}} This part adds up two parts: a rise from 3 customer-service calls upwards and a second rise from 4 calls upwards.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C079]}} From 3 calls upwards it adds to the chance slowly at first, then faster: for a typical such customer, 4 calls take it from about 3\% to about 18\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C078]}} Up to 3 calls it barely moves a typical customer's chance, which stays at about 3\%, rising slowly at first, then faster.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C077]}} Daytime minutes add to the chance only once they rise above about 221 minutes (between 186 and 221 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 3\% at 0 minutes to about 19\% at 271 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C088]}} More voice-mail messages lower it in an uneven way: for the typical customer it acts on, from about 12\% at 0 to about 6\% at 32 messages.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C080]}} Customers in Washington get less from it: about 7\% instead of about 12\% for the typical customer it acts on.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C082]}} This part reads only the state: it raises a typical customer's chance from about 3\% to about 22\% in Rhode Island, and by less than a point in Indiana.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C100, C101]}} This part reads evening minutes: nothing until about 217 minutes, then steadily, but a typical customer's chance stays at about 3\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103, C104]}} This small part reads voice-mail messages and being in Louisiana, and barely changes the predictions (by at most one point).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111]}}
\paragraph{The whole model.} The model adds up six parts into one score: fixed-weight inputs, service calls, heavy daytime use, state units, an evening unit and a small voice-mail unit.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C046]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made up of these six parts (each explained below); the score is their sum, which was checked on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C046]}} Changing one input at a time across the whole model, an international plan takes a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 3\% to about 31\%, and a voice-mail plan lowers it to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C001, C006]}} More daytime minutes raise it in an uneven way, from about 3\% at 112 minutes to about 8\% at 249 minutes, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C004]}} In Washington the chance is about 11\%, against about 3\% in West Virginia.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C002]}} The model ignores evening calls, international calls, the international charge, night-time calls, the night-time charge and night-time minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C040, C041, C042, C043, C044, C045]}}
\paragraph{Fixed-weight inputs.} This part adds up most inputs with fixed weights: an international plan, voice-mail messages, the evening charge and international minutes raise the chance of leaving, steadily for the numbers, and a voice-mail plan lowers it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C047, C049, C055, C056, C051]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, an international plan takes a typical customer from about 3\% to about 31\%, and a voice-mail plan lowers the chance to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C047, C051]}} More voice-mail messages raise it steadily, from about 3\% at 0 to about 10\% at 32 messages, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C049]}} Through it, the state moves the chance from about 3\% in West Virginia to about 11\% in Washington and about 7\% in New Jersey, and to under 1\% in Hawaii and in Rhode Island (72 to 122 training customers per state).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C048, C050, C052, C053]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C076]}}
\paragraph{Service calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving with calls to customer service from 3 calls upwards, slowly at first, then faster; it adds up two parts.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C079, C078, C077]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made of two parts that are added: calls from 3 upwards and calls from 4 upwards.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C079]}} From 3 calls upwards it adds to the chance slowly at first, then faster: for a typical such customer, 4 calls take it from about 3\% to about 18\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C078]}} Up to 3 calls it barely moves a typical customer's chance, which stays at about 3\%, rising slowly at first, then faster.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C077]}}
\paragraph{Calls from 4 upwards.} This part raises the chance of leaving from 4 customer-service calls upwards, slowly at first, then faster.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C093]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 318 of 4000 training customers, 159 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 8\% without it and about 18\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C094]}} Through it, the chance rises slowly at first, then faster: 4 calls take a typical such customer from about 3\% to about 6\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C093]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C095]}}
\paragraph{Calls from 3 upwards.} This part raises the chance of leaving from 3 customer-service calls upwards, slowly at first, then faster.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C097, C096]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on 848 of 4000 training customers, 215 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 3\% without it and about 4\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C098]}} Through it, the chance rises slowly at first, then faster: 4 calls take a typical such customer from about 3\% to about 8\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C097]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C099]}}
\paragraph{Heavy daytime use.} This part raises the chance of leaving for heavy daytime users: daytime minutes add to it only above about 221 minutes (between 186 and 221 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way, and voice-mail messages and being in Washington lower it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C088, C080, C082]}} \textit{Evidence.} This part acts on 1099 of 4000 training customers, 291 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 3\% without it and about 12\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C091]}} Daytime minutes add to the chance only once they rise above about 221 minutes (between 186 and 221 minutes for different customers), in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, from about 3\% at 0 minutes to about 19\% at 271 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C088]}} More voice-mail messages lower it in an uneven way: for the typical customer it acts on, from about 12\% at 0 to about 6\% at 32 messages.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C080]}} Customers in Washington get less from it: about 7\% instead of about 12\% for the typical customer it acts on.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C082]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C092]}}
\paragraph{State units.} This part reads only the state and raises the chance of leaving in Rhode Island, and a little in Indiana.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C100, C101]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a typical customer's chance goes from about 3\% to about 22\% in Rhode Island, and up by less than a point in Indiana.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C100, C101]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C102]}}
\paragraph{Evening unit.} This part reads evening minutes and barely changes the chance of leaving: nothing until about 217 minutes, then steadily.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103, C104]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, evening minutes change nothing until about 217 minutes, then raise the chance steadily, but a typical customer's chance stays at about 3\% from 138 to 266 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C103]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C105]}}
\paragraph{Small voice-mail unit.} This small part reads voice-mail messages and being in Louisiana, and barely changes the predictions.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a typical customer's chance stays at about 3\% in Louisiana as elsewhere, and voice-mail messages barely change it (about 3\% at 0 and at 32 messages).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C106, C107]}} Switching it off changes the predictions by at most one point.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C112]}}
\paragraph{Worth checking against what is known.} Worth checking: for customers in Rhode Island the fixed-weight inputs lower the chance to under 1\% while the state units raise it to about 22\%, so overall it stays at about 3\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C053, C100, C033]}} Worth checking: the state moves the chance by several points (Washington about 11\%, New Jersey about 7\%, Hawaii under 1\%), based on 72 to 122 training customers per state.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C002, C005, C007]}} Worth checking: the model treats a voice-mail plan as lowering the chance of leaving but more voice-mail messages as raising it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C006, C003]}} Worth checking: voice-mail messages raise the chance through the fixed-weight inputs but lower it through heavy daytime use.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C049, C080]}}

\subsection{Coverage}\label{app:churn100-s4-c2:coverage}
Coverage is computed by the current code (the function behind the \texttt{get\_coverage} tool) under these conventions. \emph{Candidate nodes} are all nodes of the explained model state except the output nodes. A candidate node is \emph{covered} when some annotation of the hierarchy (a leaf, or a composition together with its descendants) contains it and all its enabled outgoing edges. \emph{Exact Null} parts, which have no effect on any output for any input, count as covered: nodes with no path to an output over enabled, non-zero-weight edges (disconnected inputs and dead ends), and edges that have zero weight or touch such a node. Compositional coverage is the fraction of required compositions present: every annotation except a single global root containing every output must have a parent; a parentless, childless annotation made only of Null nodes is exempt.

\textbf{Hypothesis.} Root: logit P(churn) = -1.30 + linear\_\allowbreak{}backbone (identity\_\allowbreak{}lin) + service\_\allowbreak{}calls (identity\_\allowbreak{}svc) + 1.53*3118 + 1.91*10131 (day\_\allowbreak{}usage\_\allowbreak{}hinges) + 0.20*15524 (evening\_\allowbreak{}hinge) - 1.01*1295 - 1.21*7872 + 0.04*9954 (state\_\allowbreak{}offsets) + 0.005*6089, purely additive in the logit; the sigmoid is the only coupling. 37 inputs are unconnected (international charge and calls, night minutes/\allowbreak{}charge/\allowbreak{}calls,\allowbreak{} evening calls, area codes 408/510 and 29 state indicators) and have zero effect. Train AUC 0.8908, accuracy 0.888. Performance sources (train): all children replaced by least-squares linear fits gives AUC 0.8333 (an L2 logistic regression refit on all 71 inputs gets 0.8433); restoring day\_\allowbreak{}usage\_\allowbreak{}hinges alone gives 0.8707, service\_\allowbreak{}calls alone 0.8659, both 0.8907; evening, state and voicemail units restore nothing. So the gain over linear (+0.058) comes from the day-usage and service-call thresholds, which are complementary. Rare-category switches: state:11 -2.75 logit (73 rows, empirical -1.35); state:46 -1.94 (80 rows, -0.91); state:45 -0.94 (91, -0.85); state:47 +0.90 mean (72 rows, empirical +0.92; direct +1.23, but it switches off 10131 so heavy day users lose up to 2.75); state:31 +0.83 (90, +0.67); state:18 +0.41 (65 rows, empirical -0.48: opposite sign); state:39 -0.25 net (82, -0.93: direct -2.61 almost cancelled by the state units).
